payload.rationale:
For 2026 to resolve as the hottest year on record, the NASA GISS temperature anomaly must exceed both the 2025 value and 1.28 degrees Celsius. Global temperatures are heavily influenced by the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). Following the strong El Niño of 2023-2024, which spiked global temperatures, 2026 is statistically more likely to experience ENSO-neutral or La Niña conditions. These phases typically suppress global average temperatures relative to the long-term trend, making it difficult to break records set during El Niño years. While the underlying anthropogenic warming trend of approximately 0.2°C per decade continuously raises the baseline, setting a new absolute record in a likely non-El Niño year is a low-probability event. 

The strongest reason this estimate could be too high is if a prolonged La Niña establishes itself through 2026, which would virtually guarantee temperatures fall short of the 1.28°C and 2025 thresholds. The strongest reason this estimate could be too low is if the underlying global warming trend is accelerating faster than expected, or if an unexpected early return to strong El Niño conditions occurs in 2026, pushing temperatures to new extremes.
limitations: Uncertainty regarding the exact phase of ENSO in 2026.
Lack of current NASA GISS data for 2024/2025 to establish the precise baseline.
